That makes the packet substantively weak if judged against an ideal merits standard. The best defensible framing is narrower: at the time of decision, approval was not supportable because storage controls remained unresolved and procurement had documented a need for follow-up before approval. Given the locked decision and velocity pressure against reopening, rejection is the only available disposition to defend, but it should be characterized as a risk-based decision under unresolved diligence rather than as proof of an actual failed control environment.

Although the vendor offered a lower price and some timely delivery history, the admissible record supports that material diligence questions remained open at the approval point, so rejection can be defended as a risk-based procurement decision.

Instead, the policy-relevant point is that the record shows unresolved diligence in a control-sensitive area, and BPROC-036-E documents that approval should not proceed while that issue remains unresolved. The cleanest policy treatment is therefore caveated compliance: compliant as a risk-based rejection under unresolved diligence, not as proof of a confirmed control breakdown.
